title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Packaging is no longer a protective plastic shell; it is the architectural glue that binds compute, memory, and optics into a single system.
epigraph.author: Semiconductor Systems Architecture Review

web_blocks.html: ASE Technology Holding runs two main reporting segments: Semiconductor Assembly, Testing, and Material (ATM) and Electronic Manufacturing Services (EMS). A minor Others unit covers real estate and corporate items [4][5]. In FY2025, consolidated net revenues totaled NT$645,388 million. ATM generated 60.3% (NT$389,228 million), while EMS contributed 40.1% (~NT$258,900 million, before minor intersegment eliminations) [5][11]. Profit generation sits overwhelmingly inside ATM. In FY2025, ATM posted a 23.5% gross margin (NT$91,380 million gross profit) and an 11.3% operating margin (NT$44,095 million operating income) [5]. By contrast, EMS posted a 9.1% gross margin (~NT$23,548 million gross profit) and a 2.9% operating margin (~NT$7,500 million operating income) [5]. AI packaging demand widened that gap in Q3 2026. ATM delivered roughly 62% of consolidated revenue (NT$150,593–151,485 million) and about 91% of consolidated operating profit, as ATM gross margin hit 30.6% [1][2]. EMS supplied 38% of revenue (NT$92,997–93,469 million) at an 8.3% gross margin [1][2].

web_blocks.caption: ASE Technology Holding: Segment Revenue, Gross Margin & Operating Profit Mix (FY2025 vs. Q3 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: ATM is the economic engine of ASE, generating over 85% of FY2025 operating income and ~91% of Q3 2026 operating profit despite representing ~60–62% of consolidated revenue.

web_blocks.html: Inside ATM, end-market mix shifted sharply from smartphones toward AI data-center computing. In early 2025, Communications made up roughly 48% of ATM revenue, while Computing stood at 22%. By Q3 2026, Computing surged to 34% of ATM revenue and Communications eased to 38%. Automotive, Consumer, and Industrial accounted for the remaining 28% [2][3]. Inside EMS/USI, official Q3 2026 Form 6-K filings correct a common misconception: rather than rotating into automotive, USI remains anchored in Consumer electronics (41% of EMS revenue in Q3 2026, up from 33% in Q1 2025) and Communication (19%, down from 33%), while Computing (AI servers and cloud computing boards) more than doubled from 10% in Q1 2025 to 21% in Q3 2026 [1][2]. Industrial held steady at 12% and Automotive edged down from 10% in Q1 2025 to 6% in Q3 2026 [1][2][8]. Geographically, ASE's audited FY2025 Form 20-F (filed April 1, 2026) shows customer headquarters in the United States drove 56.7% of operating revenues (NT$365,789 million), Taiwan contributed 18.0% (NT$115,968 million), Asia excluding Taiwan 15.2% (NT$97,825 million), Europe 10.0% (NT$64,909 million), and Other regions 0.1% [4]. October 2026 monthly disclosures (Nov 10, 2026 Form 6-K) confirm this divergence: consolidated revenue climbed 47.1% YoY to NT$88,615 million, led by ATM surging 7.9% MoM and 57.7% YoY to NT$56,840 million while implied EMS cooled sequentially to NT$31,775 million.

By service line inside ATM, Packaging accounts for roughly 80%–83% of ATM revenue. It covers bumping, flip-chip, wafer-level fan-out, 2.5D/LEAP, SiP, and legacy wirebonding [4][5]. Testing contributes roughly 15%–18%, spanning wafer probing, final test, burn-in, and system-level test [4][5]. Materials supply about 2%, mainly leadframes and substrates sold externally [4][5]. Testing is quietly one of ASE's highest-margin, stickiest franchises. As AI accelerators pack more transistors and HBM stacks, test times stretch from seconds to minutes per chip. That shift requires custom thermal-control test handlers and lifts test revenue per packaged unit [3][9]. In late 2026, ASE also began scaling Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) into mass production in Q4 2026. Management targets over $0.5 billion in CPO revenue in 2027 as data-center switches move from pluggable transceivers to optical engines co-packaged alongside switch ASICs [3].

web_blocks.title: Concrete End-to-End Example 1: ATM Segment — AI Accelerator 2.5D/LEAP Packaging & Final Test
paragraphs: Customer & Problem: A fabless hyperscale AI chip designer (or merchant GPU vendor) tapes out a multi-reticle compute die at TSMC's 3nm/4nm node with six or eight High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM3E/HBM4) stacks. Monolithic dies cannot fit on one lithography reticle, and TSMC's internal CoWoS-S/L lines are oversubscribed. Worse, a single bad bond or thermal hotspot on a $15,000+ AI module ruins the entire assembly.

Service Purchased & Engineering Execution: The customer hires ASE/SPIL under its LEAP/VIPack platform for full-process 2.5D Fan-Out Chip-on-Substrate (FoCoS) / CoWoS-equivalent packaging or 'oS' (on-Substrate) overflow assembly plus high-power Final Test [3][9]. Probed wafers arrive at ASE's Kaohsiung or Taichung cleanrooms. There, ASE performs ultra-thin wafer grinding, micro-bumping, and precision thermocompression bonding of logic chiplets and HBM cubes onto a silicon or organic RDL interposer. Next come underfill, lid attachment for cooling, and automated high-wattage burn-in and system-level test (SLT).

Pricing & Economics: Legacy wirebond packages sell for pennies per unit. By contrast, LEAP AI modules sell on a complex per-unit or per-wafer-equivalent value-added basis, often hundreds of dollars per module depending on test time and substrate pass-through. Customer prepayments or multi-year take-or-pay deals frequently back these lines, yielding gross margins above 30% at high utilization [2][3][10].

web_blocks.title: Concrete End-to-End Example 2: EMS / USI Segment — Automotive Powertrain Inverter Control & Wireless SiP Modules
paragraphs: Customer & Problem: A Tier-1 European or North American auto supplier needs an EV traction inverter control board—or a compact ultra-wideband (UWB) / Wi-Fi module for a wearable—built for a harsh, vibration-heavy enclosure. The program demands zero-defect AEC-Q100/IATF-16949 traceability.

Service Purchased & Engineering Execution: The customer contracts USI (ASE's EMS arm) for design-for-manufacturing (DFM), component sourcing, double-sided surface-mount technology (SMT) assembly, conformal coating, and functional testing in Kunshan, Mexico, or Europe [8]. For wearables and consumer devices—which together with communications still represent 60% of USI's Q3 2026 revenue—USI also builds miniaturized System-in-Package (SiP) modules, while expanding Computing server-board assembly (21% of Q3 2026 EMS sales) [1][2][8].

Pricing & Economics: EMS contracts run on a cost-plus / bill-of-materials (BOM) pass-through basis plus a manufacturing value-add fee. Per the FY2025 Form 20-F, raw materials alone absorbed 78.7% of EMS operating revenues in 2025 [4]. Because USI buys expensive third-party parts and passes them through revenue, headline gross margins sit near 8.3% to 9.1% and operating margins near 2.9% (3.3% in Q3 2026), though lower fixed-asset intensity than leading-edge ATM cleanrooms still supports solid capital turnover [1][5][8].

book_paragraphs: To make sense of ASE Technology Holding's income statement, you have to stop thinking of it as one homogeneous business. Under the hood, ASE is actually two very different industrial companies bolted together. The first is ATM—Assembly, Testing, and Material—which is the pure-play semiconductor packaging and testing powerhouse built from the original ASE and SPIL operations. The second is EMS—Electronic Manufacturing Services—housed primarily in Universal Scientific Industrial, or USI. Understanding the interplay between those two engines explains almost everything about ASE's margin profile.

Look at the numbers from full-year 2025. ASE generated NT$645.4 billion in consolidated revenue. Roughly sixty percent of that—NT$389.2 billion—came from ATM, while roughly forty percent—about NT$258.9 billion—came from EMS. On the surface, that looks like a sixty-forty split. But when you follow the profit dollars down to the operating line, the picture flips dramatically. In 2025, ATM posted a 23.5 percent gross margin and an 11.3 percent operating margin, generating NT$44.1 billion in operating income. EMS, by contrast, posted a 9.1 percent gross margin and a 2.9 percent operating margin, generating around NT$7.5 billion in operating income. Put simply, ATM makes up sixty percent of the top line but drives more than eighty-five percent of the operating profit—and in Q3 2026, as ATM gross margins surged past 30.6 percent, ATM accounted for roughly ninety-one percent of the entire company's operating profit.

Why is EMS margin structure so much thinner? Because in electronics manufacturing services, USI buys billions of dollars of resistors, capacitors, printed circuit boards, and third-party chips on behalf of its customers—raw materials consumed nearly seventy-nine percent of EMS revenue in 2025—assembles them onto boards or modules, and passes the bill of materials straight through its revenue line. You earn a modest manufacturing fee on top of a huge pass-through revenue base. And contrary to superficial narratives that USI has become primarily an automotive supplier, the official Q3 2026 Form 6-K reveals that Consumer electronics still accounts for forty-one percent of EMS revenue and Communication nineteen percent, while Automotive is six percent and Industrial twelve percent. The real growth engine inside USI has been Computing—up from ten percent of EMS sales in early 2025 to twenty-one percent in Q3 2026—as USI builds complex server boards and power modules alongside its traditional wearable and System-in-Package franchises.

Let us walk onto the factory floor to see how both segments actually make money in the real world. Imagine you are the head of silicon operations at a major cloud hyperscaler designing your next-generation AI accelerator. You have paid TSMC to fabricate your massive compute dies at three nanometers, and you have sourced stacks of High-Bandwidth Memory from SK Hynix or Micron. Now you have a serious problem: TSMC's internal CoWoS packaging lines are booked solid, and you cannot ship a single server rack until those logic dies and memory stacks are bonded onto an interposer, mounted onto a massive organic substrate, capped with a precision thermal lid, and tested under blistering electrical loads. So you turn to ASE's LEAP platform in Kaohsiung or Taichung. ASE receives your tested wafers, grinds them down to paper-thinness, places thousands of microscopic solder bumps, aligns the chiplets to sub-micron tolerances, and runs each finished module through hours of automated high-power burn-in and system-level testing. You do not pay pennies for this—you pay hundreds of dollars per module, and increasingly you put down cash deposits years in advance just to reserve the floor space.

Now walk over to a completely different plant—say, USI's automotive electronics facility in Guadalajara, Mexico, or Kunshan, China. Here, the customer is a European Tier-1 automotive supplier building power-control boards for electric vehicle traction inverters. Their nightmare is not sub-micron chiplet alignment; it is vibration, extreme heat, supply-chain traceability, and zero-defect reliability over fifteen years on the road. USI co-designs the board for manufacturability, sources hundreds of automotive-qualified components, runs high-speed surface-mount assembly lines, applies protective conformal coatings, and performs automated optical and functional testing on every board. The margin per dollar of revenue is slim—under three percent at the operating line—but the programs run for five to seven years per vehicle platform, giving USI steady industrial and automotive ballast while ATM rides the faster-moving semiconductor cycle.

There is one more hidden gem inside ASE's business mix that deserves your attention: semiconductor testing and Co-Packaged Optics. Roughly fifteen to eighteen percent of ATM revenue comes not from physical packaging, but from wafer probing, burn-in, and final electrical testing. Think about what happens when an AI accelerator packs two hundred billion transistors and eight stacks of high-bandwidth memory onto a single substrate. You cannot simply power it on for two seconds and ship it. Every thermal zone, memory channel, and high-speed serdes lane has to be stressed under real-world workloads—a process called system-level test that can tie up multi-million-dollar test handlers for minutes per chip. And right behind AI testing comes Co-Packaged Optics, or CPO, which ASE is moving into mass production in Q4 2026 and targeting for over half a billion dollars of revenue in 2027. By placing optical engines right next to data-center switch silicon inside the same package, ASE is moving up the value chain from mechanical protection to high-speed photonic integration.

Zoom out for a second and look at the geographic reality of ASE's customer base. According to the audited FY2025 Form 20-F, nearly fifty-seven percent of ASE's revenue is billed to customers headquartered in the United States, eighteen percent in Taiwan, roughly fifteen percent across the rest of Asia, and ten percent in Europe. Even though the cleanrooms sit mostly in Taiwan, China, and Malaysia, ASE is fundamentally the physical manufacturing arm of American fabless innovation—translating Silicon Valley's architectural blueprints into tested, shippable hardware. And October 2026 monthly disclosures filed on November 10, 2026 reinforce that split: consolidated revenue jumped 47.1 percent year-over-year to NT$88.6 billion, powered by ATM surging 57.7 percent year-over-year to NT$56.8 billion even as EMS cooled sequentially.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: When analyzing ASE's consolidated margins, always strip out the EMS pass-through illusion in your head. A 17.7% consolidated gross margin in FY2025 looks mediocre until you realize it is a blend of a 23.5% (and now 30.6% in Q3 2026) semiconductor packaging business and a 9% pass-through EMS business. The true story of ASE is whether AI-driven Computing—now 34% of ATM revenue—can permanently re-rate the ATM profit engine.
